options: A. Pairing the primary metric with a guardrail metric that would degrade if the system gamed the primary.
B. Defining, in advance, the outcome the system exists to improve rather than the proxy that is easy to measure.
C. Selecting the metric on which the model already performs best across the evaluation set.
D. Deferring metric selection until the first evaluation run has shown what the model is actually capable of.
E. Adopting the same metric the previous vendor reported, so the two can be compared.
rationale: Proxy metrics are chosen because they are measurable, and systems optimise exactly what they are pointed at. Naming the real outcome first keeps the proxy accountable to something, and a guardrail metric — one that would move the wrong way if the primary were being gamed — is what makes the gaming visible. Choosing the metric the model already wins on, deferring until after results are seen, and inheriting a vendor's metric all let the measurement be selected to flatter the system.

question: Stakeholder engagement for a new AI system has consisted of interviews with the internal teams who will operate it. What is the main gap?
options: A. Operators cannot assess whether the design the team has proposed is technically feasible to build and run.
B. Interviews are a less reliable way of gathering requirements than a structured survey would be.
C. The people the system will make decisions about have not been consulted, and they experience risks operators do not.
D. The engagement was not documented in a form an external auditor would accept as evidence.
rationale: Operators know where the system is awkward to use; they do not experience being wrongly declined, or being unable to find out why. Those harms are only visible from the receiving end, which is why affected-population engagement is a distinct requirement rather than a broader version of user research. Feasibility is not what operators were asked about, method and documentation are secondary to who was in the room.

question: A training set was assembled by combining four internal databases over several years. Which characteristic most limits the team's ability to answer questions about it later?
options: A. The storage format the combined dataset uses, and how easily it can be read.
B. The total size of the combined dataset, and the storage it now occupies.
C. The number of features carried through into the final feature set.
D. The absence of lineage recording where each record came from and under what terms.
rationale: Almost every later question — may we use this, must we delete that, why does the model behave this way for one segment — resolves to where a record came from and what was permitted. Lineage is cheap to capture at assembly time and effectively unrecoverable afterwards, which is what makes its absence the binding constraint. Size, feature count and format are all tractable problems by comparison.

question: A validation set was created by randomly splitting a dataset in which the same customer appears many times. Which two problems does this create?
options: A. Records from the same customer appear in both training and validation, inflating measured performance.
B. Measured performance will not predict behaviour on customers the model has never seen.
C. The validation set will be too small for the resulting numbers to be statistically meaningful.
D. The model will overfit to whichever feature dominates the combined dataset.
E. The split will breach data minimisation, since every record is used more than once.
rationale: Random splitting assumes rows are independent, and repeated customers break that assumption: the model sees a customer in training and is then tested on the same customer, so it is being asked to recall rather than generalise. The two consequences are one problem stated twice over — the number comes out too high, and it does not describe the case the model will actually face in production. Set size, feature dominance and minimisation are unrelated to the leakage.

question: A team wants to reduce a demographic performance gap by adding more data from the under-performing group. When is this most likely to fail?
options: A. When the gap is caused by label quality rather than by sample size.
B. When the additional data is stored in a different system.
C. When the model uses a gradient-boosted architecture rather than a neural network.
D. When the additional data increases total training time.
rationale: More data fixes a representation problem, and representation is not the only cause of a gap. If the labels for that group were produced by a process that was itself unreliable or biased, additional examples supply more of the same wrong signal and can widen the gap rather than close it. Storage location, model architecture and training time affect the cost of the attempt, not whether it addresses the cause.

question: An organisation uses synthetic data to train a model where real data is scarce. Which governance question matters most?
options: A. Whether the synthetic data was generated on infrastructure the organisation has approved.
B. Whether the synthetic data reproduces the relationships the model must learn, including the rare cases.
C. Whether the synthetic data exceeds in volume the real data that was available to the team to begin with.
D. Whether the synthetic data can be told apart from real records by manual inspection.
rationale: Synthetic data inherits the assumptions of whatever generated it, and generators reproduce the common patterns far more faithfully than the tails. Since the tails are usually where the consequential failures live, fidelity on rare cases is the question that decides whether the model learns anything useful. Infrastructure, volume and inspectability are operational matters that do not bear on whether the data represents the problem.

question: A model is being retired and replaced. Which two governance actions are most important at retirement?
options: A. Retaining the records needed to explain decisions the retired model made.
B. Confirming that every downstream consumer has moved off it before it is switched off.
C. Publishing the retired model's weights so external researchers can study it.
D. Deleting every record associated with the retired model, including its decision logs.
E. Notifying the model's original vendor of the date on which it was retired.
rationale: Retirement obligations run in two directions. Backwards: decisions the model made remain live for the people they affected, who may contest them long after the model is gone, so the explanatory record has to survive it. Forwards: models acquire undocumented consumers, and switching one off without confirming who still calls it is a common outage. Publishing weights is unrelated, wholesale deletion destroys exactly what the first obligation requires, and vendor notice is a contractual detail.

question: Vantage is deciding whether to extend the safety system to its two older plants, where camera coverage is sparser. What should weigh most heavily?
options: A. Whether the vendor will discount the licence in exchange for covering two additional sites.
B. Whether the older plants have the network capacity to stream video from every camera continuously.
C. Whether the alerting model performs adequately under the conditions those plants actually present.
D. Whether workers at those plants have been consulted about where the cameras would be placed.
rationale: A system validated in one environment is not thereby validated in another, and sparser coverage changes the input the model was tuned on. If it degrades quietly in the new setting, the plant gains a safety system that reports fewer hazards than exist — worse than no system, because it is trusted. Bandwidth and pricing are feasibility questions, and consultation matters but does not answer whether the system works there.

question: An organisation is choosing between retrieval-augmented generation and fine-tuning for a policy assistant. Which two considerations most favour retrieval?
options: A. Source policies change frequently and answers must reflect the current version.
B. Users need to see which document an answer came from.
C. The assistant must respond in under fifty milliseconds to feel usable in the workflow.
D. The organisation wants to reduce the number of documents it maintains.
E. The organisation wants the model to adopt a particular writing style.
rationale: Retrieval's advantages are currency and traceability: the knowledge lives in an index that can be updated without retraining, and every answer can point at the passage behind it. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into weights, so a policy change means another training run and there is nothing to cite. Latency favours the fine-tuned model if anything, retrieval does not reduce the document estate, and style is exactly what fine-tuning is good at.

question: A team proposes an agentic system that can take actions in production systems on a user's behalf. Which factor most changes the risk profile compared with a system that only produces text?
options: A. Agentic systems require substantially more computational resources to operate at the same volume.
B. Agentic systems require more sophisticated prompting, which fewer staff can write reliably.
C. Agentic systems are harder for users to understand, so trust in them is harder to calibrate.
D. An action taken in another system has effects that cannot be reviewed before they occur.
rationale: A text output sits in front of a person who can discard it; the harm ceiling is what someone does after reading. An agent that writes to another system has already acted by the time anyone reviews, which is why agentic designs need authorisation boundaries, action logging and reversibility built in rather than added later. Compute, comprehensibility and prompt sophistication are real differences that do not change what the system can do unsupervised.

question: Meridian's vendor reports 94% detection accuracy for synthetic content. What should Meridian establish before relying on that figure?
options: A. Whether the vendor's benchmark resembles the content Meridian actually receives, and how the errors split between misses and false flags.
B. Whether 94% is higher than the figures competing detection products report for themselves.
C. Whether the vendor will contractually warrant the 94% figure for the full term of the licensing agreement, with a remedy if it is missed.
D. Whether the 94% figure has been independently audited by a third party.
rationale: A single accuracy number conceals both things Meridian needs. It was measured on some distribution of content, and if that distribution is not Meridian's the number does not transfer. It also averages two failures with opposite consequences: a missed synthetic item reaches viewers unlabelled, a false flag brands genuine footage as fake. Benchmarks against competitors, warranties and audits all take the headline figure as the thing to compare, warrant or verify.

question: A vendor declines to disclose training data sources, citing confidentiality. What is the most constructive response?
options: A. Abandon the procurement, since a model whose training data is undisclosed cannot be assessed at all.
B. Seek warranties and evidence about the properties that matter — rights to use the data, known limitations, evaluation results — rather than the sources themselves.
C. Accept the position, since the composition of a training corpus is standard trade secret material.
D. Require the vendor to disclose its training sources to an independent third party under a non-disclosure agreement before the contract is signed.
rationale: Source lists are rarely obtainable and would not, by themselves, answer the buyer's questions. What the buyer actually needs to know is whether the vendor had the rights, what the evaluation showed, and where the model is known to fail — all of which can be warranted and evidenced without naming a corpus. Walking away discards workable options, accepting silence leaves the questions unanswered, and third-party disclosure is heavy machinery for a problem that has a lighter solution.

question: An organisation is assessing the impact of a system it plans to deploy. Which two inputs make the assessment most useful?
options: A. What happens to a person when the system is wrong, and how they would find out.
B. Which groups the system will treat differently, and whether that difference is justified.
C. The number of engineers who built the system, and how long they worked on it.
D. The cloud region the system will run in, and who operates that region.
E. The projected licensing cost over the first three years, and how it scales with usage.
rationale: An impact assessment earns its place by answering questions the business case does not. The first is the consequence of error from the affected person's position, including whether they would ever know — an error nobody can detect is never corrected. The second is differential treatment and its justification, which is where discrimination exposure lives. Team size, hosting region and licensing cost belong to delivery planning.

question: A company deploys a model it built itself. Which obligation applies to it that would not apply if it had bought the same capability?
options: A. Ensuring that staff are trained to use the system and to recognise when not to rely on it.
B. Monitoring the system's performance in production and acting on it when the model degrades.
C. Accounting for the model's development — data rights, design choices and evaluation — as well as its use.
D. Informing the individuals affected by its decisions that an AI system was involved.
rationale: Training, monitoring and disclosure attach to deploying a system and are owed whoever built it. Building adds a second set of obligations on top: the organisation now holds the development record and must be able to account for where the data came from, why the design choices were made, and what the evaluation showed. Buying transfers that burden to the vendor; it does not remove any of the deployment duties.

question: A licence permits use of a model for 'internal business purposes'. The company wants to expose it in a customer-facing feature. Which two steps are indicated?
options: A. Establishing whether customer-facing use falls inside the licensed scope.
B. Checking what the licence requires or prohibits regarding output attribution and downstream use.
C. Increasing inference capacity so the model can handle customer-facing request volume.
D. Publishing the relevant licence terms on the company's own website for customers to read.
E. Registering the customer-facing feature with the industry body that lists deployed models.
rationale: Two distinct licence questions arise, and the second is the one teams forget. Scope decides whether this use is permitted at all — internal use and external service provision are commonly separated, and sometimes priced differently. Output terms decide what the company may then do with what the model produces, including attribution duties and restrictions on downstream reuse. Capacity is an engineering matter, and the remaining options describe nothing licences require.

question: What control would most directly address the way Vantage's alert data is now being used?
options: A. Increasing the alert confidence threshold, so that fewer alerts are generated and logged.
B. Extending camera coverage so that alerts are distributed more evenly across the line.
C. Replacing the vendor with one whose model produces materially fewer false positives.
D. Defining permitted uses of alert data and enforcing that boundary in access and retention.
rationale: The problem is not that the alerts are wrong; it is that data collected for one purpose has drifted into another with no decision having been taken. The control that matches is a stated boundary on use, made real by who can see the data and how long it is kept — a purpose limit nobody can enforce is a sentence in a document. Threshold tuning, a new vendor and wider coverage all change the alerts while leaving the drift untouched.

question: A deployed model's monitoring shows stable accuracy, but complaints about its decisions have tripled. Which two responses are most appropriate?
options: A. Examining whether accuracy is stable in aggregate while degrading for a particular segment.
B. Treating the complaints as a monitoring signal the current metrics do not capture.
C. Reassuring complainants that monitoring shows the model is performing correctly.
D. Retraining the model on more recent data as a precaution while the cause is investigated.
E. Raising the threshold at which the model defers a decision to a human reviewer.
rationale: Two sound-looking sources disagree, and the resolution is almost always that they are measuring different things. Aggregate stability is compatible with a segment deteriorating badly, so disaggregation is the first check. The wider lesson is that complaints are data about the deployment that the chosen metrics did not anticipate — the sort of gap monitoring cannot close by itself. Reassurance asserts the conclusion, and retraining or threshold changes act before the cause is known.

question: An organisation maps its AI controls to a voluntary framework and wants to know what the mapping is good for. Which statement is most accurate?
options: A. It organises the work and shows where coverage is thin, without attesting anything to anyone.
B. It demonstrates to a regulator that the organisation complies with applicable AI law.
C. It substitutes for an impact assessment on each individual system in the portfolio.
D. It transfers responsibility for control failures to the body that publishes the framework.
rationale: A framework mapping is an internal instrument. Its value is that it forces the organisation to say, control by control, what it actually does and where nothing is happening — which is how gaps become visible. It attests nothing, because nobody independent has looked at it. Compliance is judged by regulators against law, impact assessments are per-system work the mapping cannot replace, and publishing bodies carry no responsibility for how their framework is used.

question: Which pair of activities does the NIST AI RMF's Measure function cover, as distinct from Map?
options: A. Identifying the context of use, and cataloguing the systems in the portfolio.
B. Evaluating system performance against chosen metrics, and tracking it after deployment.
C. Setting organisational policy, and allocating accountability for AI decisions.
D. Prioritising the risks that were identified, and closing them once they have been treated.
rationale: Measure is where evaluation happens: choosing methods, applying them, and continuing to apply them once the system is live. Map is the earlier work of establishing context and what could go wrong; Govern sets policy and accountability around all of it; and prioritising and closing risks is Manage. The four are easy to blur precisely because a real programme runs them together.

question: A vendor offers its ISO/IEC 42001 certificate as evidence. Which two details most determine what that certificate is worth to the buyer?
options: A. The scope statement, which says which parts of the business the certificate covers.
B. Whether the product being bought falls inside that scope.
C. The number of auditors the certification body assigned to the engagement and for how long.
D. Whether the certificate was issued in the buyer's own jurisdiction.
E. How many other certificates the vendor holds across its business.
rationale: A management system certificate covers a stated scope and nothing beyond it, so a vendor can hold a genuine certificate that excludes the very product on the table. Reading the scope, and then checking the product sits inside it, is the whole exercise. Audit staffing, the issuing jurisdiction and a collection of other certificates say nothing about whether this purchase is covered.

question: An organisation adopts a voluntary AI framework mid-way through building a system. When is that most likely to be worth doing?
options: A. Never — a framework adopted after design has begun cannot be applied honestly.
B. Only once the system has shipped, so the assessment reflects the finished product.
C. When the remaining lifecycle still contains decisions the framework would change.
D. Only where a customer or regulator has asked for the framework by name.
rationale: Frameworks pay off where a decision is still open — evaluation design, release criteria, monitoring, the terms of deployment. Adopting one late is worth it exactly to the extent that such decisions remain, and worth little once everything is fixed. The absolute answers all substitute a rule for that judgement, and waiting for someone to demand a framework by name confuses evidence for a customer with usefulness to the team.

question: A governance lead is asked how a model card differs from an AI impact assessment, given that both are written about a system before it is deployed and both are circulated to people outside the building team. What is the essential distinction?
options: A. A model card is produced by the engineering team, while an assessment is produced by lawyers and reviewed by them.
B. A model card is required by law, while an assessment is a voluntary practice.
C. A model card is public, while an assessment must always remain confidential.
D. A model card describes the system's properties; an assessment reasons about its effects on people.
rationale: The two answer different questions. A card characterises the artefact — intended use, measured performance, known limitations — so someone else can decide whether to rely on it. An assessment reasons about consequences for the people a deployment touches, and reaches a judgement about whether to proceed and under what conditions. Authorship, publication and legal status all vary by organisation and jurisdiction, and none of them is the distinction.

question: A model's accuracy is reported as a single figure covering all users. What does that figure most obscure?
options: A. That the errors may fall almost entirely on one group of users.
B. How the model would perform if it were retrained on more recent data.
C. How much computation each individual prediction required to produce.
D. Whether the training pipeline was documented to the team's own standard.
rationale: An aggregate is a weighted average, and a group small enough in the data can be wrong nearly every time without moving it. That is why disaggregated reporting exists: the headline can look healthy while a particular population experiences a system that barely works. Retraining, compute and documentation are all real concerns, but none of them is something the aggregate figure is hiding.

question: Why does explainability matter more for some AI systems than others?
options: A. Because complex model architectures are inherently harder to describe in plain language.
B. Because the people affected need grounds to understand and contest consequential decisions.
C. Because engineering teams debug systems faster when the model can be interpreted.
D. Because regulators tend to request explanations from larger organisations first.
rationale: The demand for an explanation scales with what the decision does to someone. A recommendation nobody has to accept needs little; a refusal of credit, a job, or a benefit needs enough for the person to understand it and push back. Architecture affects how hard an explanation is to produce rather than how much is owed, debugging is an internal benefit, and regulatory attention does not track organisation size in any reliable way.

question: A team says its model is 'unbiased' because it was trained without any protected attributes. Which two problems does that claim have?
options: A. Correlated features can carry the excluded attribute into the model regardless.
B. Bias is a property of outcomes, so it is established by measurement rather than by design.
C. Excluding protected attributes measurably reduces the model's overall accuracy on the training set.
D. Protected attributes would have been required to compute the model's loss function.
E. Removing columns makes the training pipeline harder for the team to maintain.
rationale: Both halves of the claim fail. Omitting a column does not omit the information, because postcode, purchase history and employment record can reconstruct it. And the claim is the wrong shape: whether a system is biased is settled by measuring how it behaves across groups, which the team has not done. Accuracy effects, loss functions and pipeline maintenance are unrelated to whether the assertion holds.

question: What most distinguishes governing a system that recommends from governing one that decides?
options: A. A recommender processes more data per request than a decision system does.
B. A recommender is always lower risk, because its output is only advisory.
C. Where a person can still intervene, and whether that intervention is realistic.
D. Decision systems require more computing resources to operate reliably.
rationale: The distinction that governs the controls is where a human still stands in the path and whether they can genuinely act. A recommendation accepted by default, at volume, under time pressure, is a decision by another name — which is why 'advisory' is a claim to test rather than a category to rely on. Data volume and compute describe the engineering, not the exposure.

question: An AI governance committee has authority on paper but every escalation is settled by the business unit that raised it. What does this most indicate?
options: A. The committee's terms of reference need to be redrafted more precisely.
B. Escalations are reaching the committee before they have been properly prepared.
C. The committee is meeting too infrequently to keep pace with the escalations.
D. Decision rights sit with the business units, whatever the documentation says.
rationale: Authority is located by watching who actually settles things. If every escalation returns to the unit that raised it, the committee is a consultation step and the decision right never moved, which is a structural fact that no amount of redrafting changes. Cadence and preparation quality are worth attending to once the decision right is real; until then they improve the wrong thing.

question: A company is writing role descriptions for AI governance. Which two responsibilities must be held by someone named, rather than shared across a function?
options: A. Deciding whether a specific system may go into production.
B. Answering for a system's behaviour once it is operating.
C. Attending the periodic AI governance forum on the team's behalf.
D. Reviewing the annual training material for accuracy and tone.
E. Maintaining the shared library of assessment templates.
rationale: Two things fail when they are everybody's: the decision to deploy and the answer for what happens next. Both need a name, because a diffused release decision is made by whoever is least cautious, and diffused ownership means nobody is looking when a system degrades. Forum attendance, training review and template upkeep are real work that a function can hold collectively without anything falling over.

question: Two years after publishing its AI policy, a company finds most teams cannot say what it requires of them. What is the most useful first response?
options: A. Find out where teams look when they need an answer, and put the requirement there.
B. Reissue the policy with a communications campaign to raise its profile internally.
C. Add a mandatory annual attestation that each team has read the policy in full.
D. Shorten the policy so that it can be read in a single sitting by anyone.
rationale: A policy is followed where it meets the work: the intake form, the design template, the release checklist, the pull request. Teams that cannot recite it are usually telling you it lives somewhere they never go, so the fix is to move the requirement into their path rather than to push harder from outside it. Campaigns and attestations measure exposure rather than practice, and a shorter document nobody consults is still not consulted.

question: A procurement team asks governance for a single question to put to every AI vendor. Which is most revealing?
options: A. Which recognised frameworks and standards does your organisation align to?
B. Where does this system perform worst, and how did you establish that?
C. How many customers are running this system in production today?
D. What is your published roadmap for the coming twelve months?
rationale: Asking for known weaknesses tests two things at once: whether the vendor has evaluated its system seriously enough to have found the edges, and whether it will say so. A vendor that cannot answer has not looked; one that will not answer has told you how the relationship will go when something breaks. Framework alignment, customer counts and roadmaps are all answerable by a vendor that has never examined its own failure modes.

question: A company relies on legitimate interests to process personal data for model training. What does that basis additionally require?
options: A. Written approval from the supervisory authority before training may begin.
B. An opportunity for every affected individual to consent before their data is used.
C. A documented balancing of that interest against the rights of the people involved.
D. That the resulting model is never used for any commercial purpose whatsoever.
rationale: Legitimate interests is not a default that applies when consent is inconvenient — it is a basis that has to be worked for, by identifying the interest, showing the processing is necessary for it, and weighing it against what the individuals would reasonably expect. That assessment has to be recorded, because it is the thing an authority would ask to see. Prior approval is not required, consent is a different basis entirely, and commercial purposes are not excluded.

question: An AI feature will process personal data already held by the company. Which factor most determines whether a fresh notice to individuals is needed?
options: A. Whether the AI feature was built in-house or licensed from an external supplier.
B. Whether the volume of data involved exceeds the company's internal reporting threshold.
C. Whether the data was originally collected within the last twenty-four months.
D. Whether the new processing is something those individuals would reasonably have expected.
rationale: Transparency is measured against expectation. Data used for something a person would have anticipated from the original relationship needs no fresh telling; data turned to a purpose they would find surprising does, and that is exactly where notice obligations bite. Volume thresholds are internal conventions, collection age does not change what was communicated, and build-versus-buy affects who processes rather than what people were told.

question: A generative feature lets staff paste customer records into a prompt. Which two privacy obligations does that most directly engage?
options: A. Purpose limitation, because the records were collected to deliver a service.
B. Security of processing, because the content leaves the organisation's control.
C. Data portability, because customers may request a copy of their records.
D. Accuracy, because the generated text may contain factual errors.
E. Storage limitation, because prompts are retained by the internal audit log.
rationale: Pasting a record into a third-party prompt does two things at once: it uses the data for something other than what it was collected for, and it sends it somewhere the organisation no longer controls, often to a provider that may retain it. Those are the two obligations engaged by the act itself. Portability, output accuracy and log retention are genuine concerns elsewhere but are not what pasting the record triggers.

question: A processor wants to use a customer's data to improve its own AI product. What does that intention most clearly change?
options: A. It steps outside processing on instructions and needs the controller's agreement.
B. Nothing, provided the improvement work is performed on the customer's own infrastructure.
C. It requires the processor to appoint its own data protection officer immediately.
D. It obliges the processor to publish the resulting model under an open licence.
rationale: A processor acts on the controller's instructions, and improving its own product is its own purpose rather than the controller's. Deciding to do that is a step outside the processing role, which is why it needs the controller's agreement and usually a contractual term saying so — and why doing it quietly is the recurring problem in vendor arrangements. Infrastructure location does not change whose purpose is being served, and neither officer appointments nor open licensing follow from it.

question: A retailer uses an AI tool to screen candidates for warehouse roles and rejects most applicants over fifty. Which legal exposure is most direct?
options: A. Consumer protection, since the tool was marketed with unverified performance claims.
B. Employment discrimination, since the practice disadvantages a protected group.
C. Product liability, since the screening tool was supplied by an external vendor.
D. Contract law, since the vendor warranted the tool would be fair to all applicants.
rationale: The exposure follows the effect on people in a protected category, and age is protected in employment across most jurisdictions. That the decision came from a tool changes nothing about who is answerable: the employer made the hiring decision. Consumer protection reaches the vendor's marketing rather than the employer's hiring, product liability addresses defective goods causing harm, and a warranty gives the employer a claim against the vendor without curing its own liability.

question: A company fine-tunes a model on documents it licensed for internal reference only. What is the primary intellectual property concern?
options: A. That the fine-tuned model may be slower to run than the base model was.
B. That the fine-tuned model will need to be registered with a copyright office.
C. That the licence may not permit using the documents to train a model at all.
D. That the base model's own licence terms will automatically transfer to the output.
rationale: Licences grant enumerated uses, and 'internal reference' does not obviously include extracting the material into model weights that persist and can reproduce it. Whether it does is the question to answer before training rather than after. Runtime performance is unrelated, registration is not a precondition for anything here, and licence terms do not propagate automatically from a base model to what a downstream user produces.

question: An AI chatbot gives a customer incorrect information about a company's refund terms. Which two exposures are most immediate?
options: A. The company may be held to the terms its own interface stated.
B. Consumer protection exposure, if the statement is treated as misleading.
C. Copyright exposure, because the response reproduced published material.
D. Export control exposure, because the model is hosted in another country.
E. Competition exposure, because rivals publish clearer refund terms.
rationale: A chatbot on a company's own channel speaks for the company, so a customer who relied on what it said can reasonably argue the company is bound by it, and a regulator can treat a wrong statement about terms as misleading regardless of what produced it. The convenient framing — that the model made a mistake — is not a defence available to the party that deployed it. Copyright, export control and competition are not engaged by getting refund terms wrong.

question: A bank must give applicants specific reasons when it declines credit. Its new model is an ensemble that resists simple explanation. What follows?
options: A. The requirement is satisfied by telling applicants that an automated model was used.
B. The bank may substitute the model's average feature importances for individual reasons.
C. The requirement applies only where the decision was taken without any human review.
D. The bank must produce reasons for the individual outcome, or not use the model this way.
rationale: Adverse action requirements attach to the decision, not to the technique, so the choice of a model that cannot produce reasons is itself the thing that has to give. Either local explanation methods deliver reasons specific to this applicant, or the model is unsuitable for a use with this obligation. Disclosing that automation was involved is not a reason, a human in the loop does not remove the duty, and portfolio-wide importances describe the model rather than the applicant's outcome.
